passage: I'm Kavitha from the flat opposite. On Tuesday I minded little Zainab while her ammi fetched a parcel downstairs. The moment the door clicked, Zainab ran to it wailing, "Ammi! Ammi!" and pushed away the biscuit I offered. Five minutes later her ammi came back. Zainab clung to her legs, sobbed once more, then quieted on her shoulder. Soon she wriggled down and went back to her stacking cups, glancing at the door now and then.

qa.q: What did Zainab push away while her ammi was gone?
qa.a: Zainab pushed away the biscuit Kavitha offered.

qa.q: What was Zainab feeling when the door clicked shut?
qa.a: Zainab felt scared and upset that her ammi had gone, which is why she ran to the door wailing.

qa.q: How could a neighbour help a toddler like Zainab next time?
qa.a: Stay close and calm, tell Zainab that Ammi will come back soon, and let her stay near the door if she wants, without pushing the biscuit.

qa.q: How might Zainab's ammi see the moment she walked back in?
qa.a: Her ammi probably felt touched to be missed so strongly, and reassured when Zainab calmed and went back to playing.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler crying and clinging when her mother leaves, then calming on her return and going back to play.

passage:
Monday: At the crèche gate, Lavanya clung to Amma's sari and screamed when Amma walked away. Afreen, the crèche teacher, held her while she cried for a long time.
Wednesday: Lavanya cried again at the gate but stopped sooner and let Afreen show her the sand tray.
The next Monday: She waved a small, wobbly bye. When Amma came at noon, Lavanya ran into her arms, laughed, then tugged her back to see the sand castle.

qa.q: What did Afreen show Lavanya on Wednesday?
qa.a: Afreen showed Lavanya the sand tray.

qa.q: Why did Lavanya run into Amma's arms at noon?
qa.a: Lavanya felt happy and relieved to see Amma again; feeling safe, she then wanted to show off her sand castle.

qa.q: What small step would help Lavanya on hard mornings?
qa.a: A short, warm goodbye from Amma and the same kind teacher waiting each day help Lavanya learn that Amma always comes back.

qa.q: How might Amma have felt walking away from the gate on Monday?
qa.a: Amma may have felt torn and worried hearing Lavanya scream, and later glad to see her settle a little more each day 🙂

grounding: Shows a toddler's distress at her mother leaving easing over days, with calm reunions and a return to exploring.

passage: I'm Minakshi, Sudha's big sister. When my new tuition aunty came to our flat to meet Mummy, Sudha pressed against Mummy's knee and stared, thumb in her mouth. The aunty smiled but didn't reach for her. Mummy laughed and chatted, pouring tea. Sudha kept looking from Mummy's face to the aunty's. After a while she crept closer, held out a red block, and ran back. By the time the tea was finished, she was sitting on the rug near the aunty's feet.

qa.q: What did Sudha hold out to the tuition aunty?
qa.a: Sudha held out a red block.

qa.q: Why did Sudha keep looking from Mummy's face to the aunty's?
qa.a: Sudha felt wary of the stranger and was checking Mummy's face; seeing Mummy relaxed and laughing helped her feel safe enough to come closer.

qa.q: What did the tuition aunty get right with Sudha?
qa.a: The aunty smiled but did not reach for her, letting Sudha warm up at her own pace.

qa.q: How might the tuition aunty see Sudha's quick dash back to Mummy?
qa.a: The aunty probably saw it as ordinary shyness and felt pleased that Sudha had offered the block at all.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler staying close to her mother and watching a stranger, warming up because her mother is relaxed.

passage:
Day one: When Ankita, the new babysitter, arrived, Avni hid behind Papa's legs and watched her with round eyes. Papa sat on the floor and chatted with Ankita, easy and smiling. Avni stayed pressed to him.
Day three: Avni peeped out when Ankita blew bubbles, then looked up at Papa. He grinned, so she reached for one.
The next week: Avni toddled to the door when the bell rang and handed Ankita her doll.

qa.q: What did Ankita blow on day three?
qa.a: Ankita blew bubbles.

qa.q: Why did Avni look up at Papa before reaching for a bubble?
qa.a: Avni still felt a little unsure of Ankita and checked Papa's face; his grin reassured her that it was safe.

qa.q: How did Papa help Avni warm up?
qa.a: Papa stayed relaxed, sitting on the floor chatting and smiling with Ankita, so Avni could see she was safe, without being pushed.

qa.q: What might it be like for Ankita on the first day?
qa.a: Ankita may have felt a bit awkward being stared at, but hopeful because Papa was friendly and gave Avni time 😊

grounding: Shows a toddler's wariness of a new babysitter easing over days as she reads her father's relaxed manner.

passage: On the veranda of their house by the paddy fields, Thomas's big sister Leela, six, snatched his wooden bullock cart. Thomas, two, shrieked, grabbed her arm and bit it. Leela howled. Ammachi set down the rice she was cleaning and knelt between them. "Thomas, you're angry. Leela took your cart. You can be angry. Biting hurts, so no biting." She held his hands gently. "Say, 'Mine! Give!'" Thomas stamped and shouted, "Mine!" Ammachi turned to Leela. "Give it back, then ask for a turn."

qa.q: What did Ammachi set down before kneeling?
qa.a: Ammachi set down the rice she was cleaning.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when Leela snatched his cart?
qa.a: Thomas felt angry and frustrated that his cart was taken, which is why he shrieked and bit Leela.

qa.q: Which choice by Ammachi worked, and why?
qa.a: Ammachi named Thomas's anger, said being angry is fine but biting is not, and gave him words to use, so he learned a safer way to protest.

qa.q: How does Leela see the moment when Ammachi tells her to give the cart back?
qa.a: Leela may feel it is unfair after being bitten, but she also learns that snatching was not okay and that asking for a turn works better.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler biting when an older sibling takes a toy, and an adult naming the anger while ruling out hurting.

passage: In their small apartment in São Paulo, Priscila's big sister Lucia, seven, took the toy xylophone to show a friend on a video call. Priscila, two, screamed, "No! Mine!" and smacked Lucia's leg with the stick. Papai scooped Priscila up. "You're really angry. Lucia took it without asking. Angry is okay. Hitting is not." Priscila's face was red, her fists tight. Papai held her until her breathing slowed, then said, "Lucia, can she have it back when your call ends?" Lucia nodded, and Priscila waited on Papai's lap.

qa.q: What did Priscila smack Lucia's leg with?
qa.a: Priscila smacked Lucia's leg with the stick.

qa.q: What do Priscila's red face and tight fists suggest?
qa.a: They suggest Priscila was very angry that her xylophone was taken without asking.

qa.q: What could Papai try next time, before hitting happens?
qa.a: Papai could step in as soon as Lucia takes a toy, name Priscila's anger early and help Lucia ask first.

qa.q: How might Lucia see Priscila's anger?
qa.a: Lucia may feel surprised and hurt by the smack, yet also see that taking the xylophone without asking upset her little sister.

grounding: Shows a toddler hitting out when an older sister takes a toy, and a parent labelling the anger while holding that hitting is not allowed.

passage:
Sunday: When baby Ishita reached for the rattle, her big sister Noor, two, clutched it and turned away. Ishita cried; Noor watched her, frowning.
Tuesday: Ishita wailed in her cot. Noor toddled over, patted her tummy the way Ammi did, and said, "Shh, shh."
Friday: Ishita cried for the rattle again. Noor looked at it, looked at her sister, and pushed it through the cot bars. Ammi clapped softly. "You helped Ishita feel better."

qa.q: What did Noor push through the cot bars on Friday?
qa.a: Noor pushed the rattle through the cot bars.

qa.q: What was Noor feeling on Tuesday when she patted Ishita's tummy?
qa.a: Noor seemed concerned about her crying sister and wanted to comfort her, copying the gentle way Ammi does it.

qa.q: How did Ammi encourage Noor's gentleness?
qa.a: Ammi clapped softly and named what Noor did, which helps Noor feel proud and want to be gentle again.

qa.q: What might the moment be like for baby Ishita when the rattle comes through the bars?
qa.a: Ishita likely feels comforted and happy to have the rattle, and her crying settles 🙂

grounding: Illustrates a toddler slowly moving from guarding a toy to handing it to a crying baby sibling, an early seed of empathy.

passage: In their flat in a Pune housing society, Sangeeta, almost three, was feeding her doll when her baby brother Pankaj crawled over and grabbed the doll's spoon. Sangeeta pulled it back. Pankaj toppled onto the mat and burst into tears. Sangeeta stared at him. Then she picked up her squeaky duck and held it out. "Baby, duck," she said, patting his head a bit too hard. Mumma, watching from the kitchen door, smiled and came to show her a softer pat.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta hold out to Pankaj?
qa.a: Sangeeta held out her squeaky duck.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta offer the duck after Pankaj cried?
qa.a: Sangeeta seemed upset to see him cry and wanted him to feel better, an early sign of caring.

qa.q: How could Mumma support Sangeeta's kindness?
qa.a: Mumma can praise the offer of the duck and gently show a softer pat, so Sangeeta learns to comfort without hurting.

qa.q: How might Pankaj experience his sister's offer?
qa.a: Pankaj probably feels comforted by the squeaky duck, even if the pat was a bit rough.

grounding: Shows a toddler responding to a crying baby brother by offering a toy and a pat, the first signs of gentleness and sharing.

passage: In Grandpa Bao's backyard in Sydney, Leila, two, heard the gate click and ran to him with her arms up. He lifted her, and she pressed her cheek to his and gave him a wet kiss. When he sat on the garden bench, she climbed straight onto his lap and pushed her toy koala into his hands. "Koala for you," she said. Grandpa Bao made the koala dance, and Leila leaned back against his chest, giggling.

qa.q: What did Leila push into Grandpa Bao's hands?
qa.a: Leila pushed her toy koala into his hands.

qa.q: What was Leila feeling when she ran to Grandpa Bao with her arms up?
qa.a: Leila felt excited and happy to see him 😊 and wanted to be picked up and close.

qa.q: What small thing helps a toddler like Leila learn warmth?
qa.a: When Grandpa Bao receives her kiss and koala gladly and plays along, Leila learns her affection is welcome.

qa.q: How might Grandpa Bao feel when Leila hands him the koala?
qa.a: Grandpa Bao likely feels loved and touched that she chose to share her favourite toy.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler seeking a grandparent's lap, giving a kiss and a toy, and learning warmth by having it received.

passage: I'm Gautam, Lokesh's cousin, and I was there when Dadi came back from her village last Sunday. Lokesh, just two, peeped at her from behind the curtain at first. Then Dadi opened her arms and said, "Aa ja, mere laddoo." He trotted over, let her hug him, and pressed his nose to her cheek. A minute later he fetched his plastic truck, dropped it in her lap and climbed up after it. He stayed there, sucking his thumb, until he fell asleep.

qa.q: What did Lokesh drop in Dadi's lap?
qa.a: Lokesh dropped his plastic truck in her lap.

qa.q: Why did Lokesh climb into Dadi's lap and stay there?
qa.a: Lokesh felt safe and fond of Dadi after her warm welcome and wanted to be close; falling asleep there shows how comfortable he was.

qa.q: What did Dadi do that helped Lokesh come to her?
qa.a: Dadi opened her arms and called him warmly but let him walk over himself, so the hug was his choice.

qa.q: How might Dadi see the plastic truck landing in her lap?
qa.a: Dadi likely sees it as a small gift of love and feels delighted to be welcomed home.

grounding: Shows a toddler accepting a grandmother's hug, offering a toy and settling in her lap as her warmth is received.

passage: At the village fair near Wardha, Chandrika Mausi, visiting after two years, bent down with open arms. "Come to Mausi, Damini!" Damini, two, hid behind Amma's legs and buried her face in the sari. Mausi reached around to lift her, and Damini began to whimper. Amma put a hand on Mausi's arm. "Give her time." Mausi sat back and bought a paper windmill, blowing on it slowly. Soon Damini peeped out, watched it spin, and edged closer, one step at a time.

qa.q: What did Mausi buy at the fair?
qa.a: Mausi bought a paper windmill.

qa.q: What was Damini feeling when Mausi reached around to lift her?
qa.a: Damini felt shy and frightened of this unfamiliar Mausi, so she whimpered and hid in Amma's sari.

qa.q: Which choice helped Damini, and why?
qa.a: Amma asked Mausi to give her time, and Mausi played with the windmill instead of grabbing, letting Damini come closer at her own pace.

qa.q: How might Chandrika Mausi feel when Damini hides?
qa.a: Mausi may feel a little hurt after two years away, but can understand the hiding as shyness, not rejection.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler hiding from an unfamiliar aunt, and how giving time instead of forcing contact lets her approach.

passage: At her grandmother's birthday lunch in Madrid, Ines, two, met Uncle Felix for the first time. He was tall and loud, and she hid behind Mamá's chair, gripping Mamá's skirt. "Give your uncle a kiss," Abuela called. Mamá shook her head. "She can say hello when she's ready." Felix sat on the floor instead and rolled a small ball toward the chair. Ines watched. On the third roll, she pushed it back. By dessert she was sitting beside him, sharing a slice of cake.

qa.q: Who called out for Ines to give a kiss?
qa.a: Abuela called, "Give your uncle a kiss."

qa.q: Why did Ines grip Mamá's skirt?
qa.a: Ines felt shy and unsure of the tall, loud uncle she had never met, so she held on to Mamá for safety.

qa.q: What did Uncle Felix try that built Ines's confidence?
qa.a: He sat on the floor and rolled a ball, letting Ines choose when to join in, which helped her feel safe.

qa.q: How might Abuela see Mamá's refusal to push the kiss?
qa.a: Abuela may feel a little surprised or corrected at first, but can see Ines settling beside Felix by dessert.

grounding: Shows a toddler hiding from an unfamiliar uncle, and how refusing forced affection and letting her approach builds confidence.

passage: At the weekly market in their kasba, Pradeep, two, pointed at the stacked sugarcane and shouted, "That!" Appa shook his head. "Not today, kanna." Pradeep flung himself onto the dusty ground, kicking and wailing. Ayesha, who sold bangles at the next stall, looked over. Appa squatted beside him, voice low. "You're cross. You really wanted sugarcane. We're not buying it today." He waited without scolding. Pradeep's wails slowed to hiccups. After a while he climbed into Appa's arms and pointed at a passing goat instead.

qa.q: What did Pradeep point at in the market?
qa.a: Pradeep pointed at the stacked sugarcane.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he flung himself onto the ground?
qa.a: Pradeep felt frustrated and angry at being told no about the sugarcane he wanted.

qa.q: Which choice helped Pradeep calm down sooner?
qa.a: Appa stayed calm, named the feeling as cross, kept to "not today" and waited without scolding, so the storm passed faster.

qa.q: How does Appa experience the tantrum in the busy market?
qa.a: Appa may feel embarrassed with people like Ayesha watching, yet chooses patience over giving in.

grounding: Illustrates a toddler's tantrum at a refusal and a father who stays calm, names the feeling and holds the limit.

passage: At a playground in Berlin, the sky was darkening when his mama, Rosa, said, "Time to go home, Siddiq." Siddiq, two, clung to the swing chains and screamed, "No! More!" When she lifted him out, he arched his back and hit her shoulder. Rosa held him close, keeping her voice soft. "You're so angry. You love the swings. We're still going home." Siddiq sobbed into her coat. Rosa didn't argue or bargain. By the corner of the street, he was quiet, pointing at a bus.

qa.q: What did Siddiq cling to when it was time to leave?
qa.a: Siddiq clung to the swing chains.

qa.q: What was Siddiq feeling when he arched his back?
qa.a: Siddiq felt furious and frustrated about leaving the swings he loved.

qa.q: What did Rosa do that helped Siddiq recover?
qa.a: Rosa kept her voice soft, named his anger and his love of the swings, and still went home without bargaining.

qa.q: How might Rosa feel when Siddiq hits her shoulder?
qa.a: Rosa may feel tired and a little hurt, but stays steady because she knows he is overwhelmed, not being cruel.

grounding: Shows a toddler's tantrum on being told it is time to leave, and a mother who stays calm, names the anger and keeps the limit.

passage: In the block corner of their preschool in Lucknow, Divyansh and Payal both grabbed the one red dumper truck. "Mine!" Divyansh shouted, yanking it to his chest. Payal yanked back, and a wheel popped off. Both started crying. Ms Rekha knelt down with the loose wheel. "Two friends, one truck. What could we do?" Divyansh sniffed. "I have it first, then Payal?" "For how long?" asked Ms Rekha. They settled on the sand timer. When it ran out, Divyansh handed the truck over, and Payal let him load her blocks.

qa.q: What broke when Payal yanked the truck back?
qa.a: A wheel popped off.

qa.q: Why did Divyansh shout "Mine!" and yank the truck?
qa.a: Divyansh wanted the red truck badly and felt angry that Payal grabbed it too.

qa.q: How did Ms Rekha help the two friends?
qa.a: She asked them what they could do instead of deciding for them, then helped them use a sand timer to take turns.

qa.q: How does Payal see it when Divyansh hands over the truck?
qa.a: Payal probably feels happy and treated fairly, which is why she lets him load her blocks.

grounding: Illustrates a child shouting "mine" in a toy fight and being guided by a teacher to take turns instead of grabbing.

passage: I'm Smita, Manoj's big sister, and I was on the colony bench when Manoj and Chinmay started fighting over a remote-control car. "It's mine!" Manoj yelled, clutching the remote. Chinmay grabbed the car itself and ran. I didn't know who had it first. Our neighbour Mr Joseph called them over. "You've got the remote, Chinmay has the car. Neither works alone. Any ideas?" Manoj frowned for a long time. Then he said, "You drive it to the gate, then I drive it back?" Chinmay nodded, and they raced off together.

qa.q: What were Manoj and Chinmay fighting over?
qa.a: They were fighting over a remote-control car.

qa.q: What was Manoj thinking about when he frowned for a long time?
qa.a: Manoj was likely torn between wanting to keep the remote and wanting to play with Chinmay, and was working out a fair deal.

qa.q: What did Mr Joseph do that worked?
qa.a: He pointed out that neither part worked alone and asked the two friends for ideas, so they found their own deal instead of grabbing.

qa.q: How does Chinmay see Manoj's idea?
qa.a: Chinmay probably feels relieved and happy, since the deal lets them both drive instead of fighting.

grounding: Shows a child shouting "mine" over a shared toy and, with a neighbour's question, finding a turn-taking deal instead.

passage:
Observation note, UKG, Tuesday (Teacher Sarala)
During free play, Omkar and Kamal were building a train track. Kamal ran out of curved pieces and his face fell; he began to walk away. Omkar held out two curved pieces from his own pile: "You can have these, then we can make it go round." Kamal came back. Ten minutes later Kamal gave Omkar his only engine to push first. Omkar beamed and hugged him. 😊
Next step: I praised both boys for sharing and will pair them again on Thursday.

qa.q: What did Omkar hold out to Kamal?
qa.a: Omkar held out two curved pieces from his own pile.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling when Kamal gave him the engine?
qa.a: Omkar felt happy and warm, shown by his beaming smile and hug, because his friend shared back.

qa.q: What could Teacher Sarala keep doing to build sharing?
qa.a: Keep praising sharing as it happens and pair friends like Omkar and Kamal on building tasks, as planned for Thursday.

qa.q: How does Kamal see the moment Omkar offers the curved pieces?
qa.a: Kamal probably feels relieved and included, since he had been about to walk away.

grounding: Illustrates a child offering pieces to keep play going and feeling the warmth of reciprocity when the friend shares back.

passage: Under the neem tree near their village well, Vikas and Yamini were taking turns with his wooden lattoo, but Yamini couldn't make it spin and started to sulk. Vikas held out the string. "You keep it for three spins. I'll wind it for you." Yamini tried, and on the third go the top whirred across the dust. She shrieked with joy. Then she pulled her clay whistle from her pocket and gave it to him. "Your turn with mine." Vikas blew it loudly, grinning so hard his cheeks hurt.

qa.q: How many spins did Vikas offer Yamini?
qa.a: Vikas offered her three spins.

qa.q: Why was Vikas grinning so hard at the end?
qa.a: Vikas felt delighted and warm 😊 because Yamini shared her clay whistle after he shared the lattoo.

qa.q: What small step helped keep the game going?
qa.a: Vikas held out the string and offered to wind the top, so Yamini could join in instead of sulking.

qa.q: How does Yamini see Vikas's offer?
qa.a: Yamini likely feels encouraged and grateful, which makes her want to share her whistle in return.

grounding: Shows a child sharing a toy to keep play going and feeling warmth when the friend shares back.

passage:
Monday: At recess, Sunaina's group was playing house. "You can't play, Kamal. It's only for us." Kamal's lip wobbled. He kicked their play kitchen over and ran off.
Wednesday: The same words again. This time Kamal went to Mrs D'Souza, eyes wet. She knelt. "Tell me with words." "I feel sad. They said no." She nodded. "That hurts. Let's find someone else to play with." She walked him to the sandpit, where two children were digging a river.
Friday: Kamal ran straight to the sandpit and shouted, "I'll dig the bridge!"

qa.q: Where did Mrs D'Souza walk Kamal on Wednesday?
qa.a: She walked him to the sandpit.

qa.q: What was Kamal feeling when his lip wobbled on Monday?
qa.a: Kamal felt hurt and sad at being left out, and the hurt turned into anger when he kicked the kitchen over.

qa.q: How did Mrs D'Souza help Kamal on Wednesday?
qa.a: She asked for words, named the hurt, and walked him to another group, so Kamal found play without hitting back.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's group have seen Kamal kicking over their kitchen?
qa.a: They probably felt scared and cross, and might have been even less willing to let him play.

grounding: Illustrates a child hurt at being told he cannot play, who learns to name the hurt and, with adult help, joins another group.

passage: Rain had trapped all the children indoors at the housewarming, and the power had just gone out. By candlelight, Naveen and his cousins guarded their pile of building blocks. "You can't play, Lokesh. You're too little." Lokesh clenched his fist and raised it. Nani caught his hand gently. "You're hurt. Can you say it?" "They won't let me," he said, tears spilling. "That feels bad," Nani said. With the lights out there wasn't much else to do, so she picked up a torch. "Shall we make shadow animals? Anyone can come." Two small children joined. Soon Lokesh's shadow dog was barking on the wall.

qa.q: What did Nani pick up after the lights went out?
qa.a: Nani picked up a torch.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling when he clenched his fist?
qa.a: Lokesh felt hurt and angry at being called too little and shut out of the blocks.

qa.q: How did Nani help Lokesh instead of letting him hit?
qa.a: Nani held his hand gently, asked him to say the hurt in words, named it, and started a new game anyone could join.

qa.q: How might Naveen see Lokesh raising his fist?
qa.a: Naveen might feel startled and defensive, and could hold on to the blocks even more tightly.

grounding: Shows a child left out of play and close to hitting back, helped by an adult to put the hurt into words and find another game.
